props.title: Power

sections.content: **Power** (1986) marked a pivotal moment in political campaign films, with Richard Gere portraying Pete St. John, an amoral media consultant who manipulates public opinion for profit. Director Sidney Lumet, fresh off tackling media manipulation in **Network** (1976), turned his lens to the emerging world of professional political consultants. The film eerily predicted today's data-driven campaigning and media manipulation tactics. Like The Candidate (1972) before it, Power strips away democratic idealism to expose the cynical machinery beneath elections.

sections.content: Lumet's unflinching examination of political marketing builds on earlier works like **All the King's Men** (1949) while anticipating modern films like **The Ides of March** (2011). The film's focus on polling, focus groups, and media manipulation feels especially prescient in our era of targeted messaging and social media campaigns. Gere's consultant character became a template for later political fixers like the ones in **Thank You for Smoking** (2005) and **Miss Sloane** (2016).

The film's technical innovations in depicting media manipulation - rapid-cut montages of campaign ads, behind-the-scenes polling operations, and backroom dealings - influenced later political thrillers. **Game Change** (2012) and **Our Brand Is Crisis** (2015) borrowed heavily from Power's visual language for showing how public opinion gets shaped by unseen hands. sections.content: Power arrived at a crucial moment when political consulting was becoming a big-money industry. The film bridges classic political dramas like **The Best Man** (1964) and modern data-driven campaign narratives like **The Campaign** (2012). Its depiction of focus groups and demographic targeting predicted the Cambridge Analytica era decades early. The film's cynical view of democracy-for-hire resonates even more strongly in today's environment of micro-targeted ads and social media manipulation.
